L194: ## Abstract
L195: 
L196: ### BACKGROUND
L197: 
L198: Short, 21-mer, double-stranded/small interfering RNAs (ds/siRNAs) were designed to target bcr-abl mRNA in chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) with a potential also to target c-abl mRNA.
L199: ### METHODS
L200: ds/siRNAs were transfected into bcr-abl-positive K-562 cells (derived from blast-crisis) or bcr-abl-negative/c-abl-positive Jurkat cells (derived from acute lymphoblastic leukemia) using lipofectamine. ds/siRNAs intracellular uptake was detected by fluorescent confocal microscopy using fluorescein-labeled ds/siRNAs. The treatment was performed over 6 days with repetitive siRNA transfections.
L201: Efficiency of the siRNAs was determined 24 hours after single siRNA transfection and 6 days after repetitive siRNA transfections.
L202: ### RESULTS
L203: Two of the designed ds/siRNAs decreased the target mRNA levels markedly (determined by reverse transcriptase-polymerase chain reaction analysis) and bcr-abl/c-abl oncoproteins (determined by flow cytometry using Fluor-488-labeled, anti-c-abl antibody as well as by Western blot analysis). These sequences also inhibited protein tyrosine kinase activity significantly and suppressed cell proliferation.
L204: One of the three selected ds/siRNAs expressed only slight effects on the bcr-abl/c-abl mRNA in K-562 cells (but not on the oncoprotein level), on protein tyrosine kinase activity, and on cell proliferation. The combination of the three ds/siRNA constructs provoked stronger decreases in bcr-abl/c-abl mRNAs and their respective oncoproteins and produced the strongest suppression of cell proliferation.
L205: ### CONCLUSIONS
L206: 
L207: The cross-talk between siRNA interference of bcr-abl oncogene and the expression of several apoptotic/antiapoptotic factors, cell proliferation factors, and other oncogenes exists and it was determined by microarray analysis in K-562 cells that were treated over 6 days. Cancer 2004. © 2004 American Cancer Society.
L208: The bcr-abl oncogene is a result of a reciprocal translocation between the long arms of chromosomes 9 and 22 (known as the Philadelphia [Ph] chromosome [t(9;22)]) that encodes a cytoplasmic, chimeric fusion oncoprotein with constitutive tyrosine kinase activity, which inhibits apoptosis and triggers malignant transformation.
L209: There is good experimental evidence demonstrating that bcr-abl fusion is a single, causative abnormality in chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML), at least in chronic phase, making it a unique model for the development of molecular targets for disease control.cite21†1 -cite22†3 Gene or protein targeting of chimeric fusion is a promising way to eliminate the bcr-abl-positive cells specifically, without any influence on the viability of normal cells.
L210: Increasing knowledge of bcr-abl has resulted in the design of several novel therapeutic approaches, including highly specific tyrosine kinase inhibitors (e.g., imatinib and pyrido[2,3-d]pyrimidine derivative PD180970), single-stranded antisense oligo-RNA and oligo-DNA substances, and immunomodulation.cite21†1 -cite23†4 Recently, it has been reported that short, double-stranded RNA molecules (dsRNAs) targeted to bcr-abl abnormalities also are a promising tool for the control of chimeric fusion protein expression.cite24†5 -cite25†7 L211: It is known that dsRNAs trigger a complex gene-silencing mechanism, called RNA interference, which was discovered originally in simpler organisms (such as nematodes, plants, and Drosophila).cite26†8 -cite27†10 Once in the cell, the dsRNAs are processed into short, 21–22-mer dsRNAs by RNase III enzyme Dicer, and these short fragments serve as guide sequences to induce target-specific mRNA cleavage by the RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC).cite28†11 -cite29†13 It has been observed that this mechanism is extremely potent and requires only a few dsRNA molecules per cell to silence homologous mRNA expression.
L212: Three years ago, this mechanism also was described for mammalian cells, including human cells,cite30†14 , cite31†15 and efforts were directed toward the application of this natural phenomenon for specific influence of oncogene and oncoprotein expression.
L213: In the current report, we describe the effects of three originally designed, anti-bcr-abl/c-abl ds/small interfering RNA (ds/siRNA) constructs on the bcr-abl/c-abl mRNA and protein expression, bcr-abl/c-abl protein tyrosine kinase activity and proliferation index in bcr-abl-positive K-562 cells and bcr-abl-negative/ c-abl positive Jurkat cells.
L214: The cross-talk between siRNA interference of bcr-abl oncogene and expression of several apoptotic/antiapoptotic factors, cell proliferation factors, and other oncogenes also was investigated using microarray analysis.
L215: ## MATERIALS AND METHODS
L216: ### siRNA Constructs
L217: Twenty-one-nucleotide, ds/siRNA constructs were synthesized chemically (Genenet Company Ltd., Fukuoka, Japan). They were directed against human bcr-abl fusion peptide (major breakpoint, abl gene) and against c-abl. The sense cyclic DNA (cDNA) sequence was between exons 548 and 843 (number 3; abl gene) for siRNA-1 and siRNA-3 and between exons 374 and 547 (number 2; abl gene) for siRNA-2 (GenBank accession numbers AJ131466.1 and X16416.1, respectively).
L218: The ds/siRNA constructs correspond to nucleotide sites that are localized in the breakpoint cluster region (b3a2 junction) in the 9:22 chromosomal translocation (Ph chromosome). ds/siRNA-4 is a nonsense sequence and did not demonstrate homology with cDNAs of c-abl or bcr-abl genes. The sense mRNA/cDNA target sequences and antisense siRNA sequences are shown in Figure cite32†1 A.
L219: The following mismatch ds/siRNA construct (nonsense) was used as a negative control: siRNA-4-r(GUUUGUCAGAGUCGGACAG)d(TT)/r(CUGUCCGACUCUGACAAAC)d(TT).
L220: Figure 1
L221: 
L222: cite18†Open in figure viewer cite33†PowerPoint L223: 
L224: Sequences of chemically synthesized anti-bcr-abl, double-stranded, small interfering RNAs (ds/siRNAs) and their sense (s) and antisense (as) mRNA/cDNA target sequences. TT indicates the deoxythydimidine dimmer as 3′ overhang.
L225: ### Cells and Transfection Protocol
L226: Bcr-abl-positive K-562 cells (derived from patients with CML in blast crisis) and bcr-abl-negative/c-abl positive Jurkat cells (derived from patients with acute lymphoblastic leukemia) were a generous gift from Dr. J. Minowada (Hayashibara Biochemical Laboratories, Inc., Okayama, Japan). The cells were cultured in RPMI-1640 medium, supplemented with 10% heat-inactivated fetal bovine serum in a humidified atmosphere at 37 °C with 5% carbon dioxide.
L227: The cells used for transfection were at approximately 80% confluence.
L228: ### Transfection Conditions
L229: Cells were collected by centrifugation, resuspended in a new medium to 8 × 10^{5} cells/mL, subjected to ds/siRNA (180 nM) transfection using lipofectamine (6-hour incubation in RPMI-1640 medium in the presence of 10 U/mL RNase inhibitor; Roche Laboratories, Tokyo, Japan), replaced in a new medium (4 × 10^{5} cells/mL), and cultivated in a humidified atmosphere.
L230: The conditions for the preparation of ds/siRNA-lipofectamine complexes are described in the Lipofectamine 2000 protocol (Invitrogen, La Jolla, CA). Transfection efficacy was analyzed using a lamin A/C system (RNAi starter kit; Qiagen Inc., Chatsworth, CA).
L231: The half-life of ds/siRNAs in RPMI-1640 medium during transfection was analyzed by gel electrophoresis using ultraviolet detection and by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) using fluorescein-labeled ds/siRNA and fluorimetric detection. The cells were also subjected to “chronic treatment” with ds/siRNAs using three repetitive transfections.
L232: ### Confocal Microscopy—ds/siRNAs Intracellular Uptake
L233: Cells (2 × 10^{5} cells/mL) were transfected with fluorescein-labeled ds/siRNA (single dose, 180 nM; Qiagen Inc.) using lipofectamine as described earlier. A 6-hour transient transfection was applied, and transfected cells were cultured in RPMI-1640 medium.
L234: At different times of posttransfection (1 hour, 2 hours, 4 hours, 6 hours, and 8 hours), aliquots of the cells were sedimented by centrifugation at × 1000 g for 10 minutes; washed twice with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) (Ca^{2+} and Mg^{2+} free) to eliminate free fluorescent ds/siRNA molecules outside the cells; and the FITC-labeled ds/siRNAs, incorporated into the living cells (green light), were detected by fluorescent confocal microscopy.
L235: The samples were analyzed under an Olympus IX70 microscope (Olympus America, Inc., Melville, NY).
L236: ### mRNA Isolation
L237: mRNA was isolated from ds/siRNA-treated or untreated cells using a QuickPrep mRNA purification kit (Amersham Pharmacia Biotech, Piscataway, NJ) according to the manufacturer's instructions. The method combines the disruptive and protective properties of guanidinium thiocyanate (GTC) with the speed and selectivity of oligo(dT)-cellulose chromatography in a spun column.
L238: Briefly, total RNA was extracted in a buffered solution containing a high concentration of GTC and N-lauroyl sarcosine, which ensured the rapid inactivation of endogenous RNase and the complete dissociation of cellular components from the mRNA.
L239: The extracts were then diluted 3-fold with elution buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl [pH 7.5] and 1 mM ethylenediamine tetraacetic acid [EDTA]) to reduce the GTC concentration low enough to allow efficient hydrogen bonding between poly(A) tracts on mRNA molecules and oligo(dT) attached to cellulose but high enough to maintain complete inhibition of RNases. This 3-fold dilution also caused precipitation of some proteins, which were removed by centrifugation at × 12,000 g for 10 minutes.
L240: The supernatant fluid was poured into an oligo(dT)-cellulose spun column, and the polyadenylated fraction was allowed to bind over a short period with gentle mixing (10 minutes). The column was subjected to low-speed centrifugation (× 350 g for 2 minutes); and the liquid, which contained the nonbound material, was decanted. The matrix was batch-washed sequentially with high-salt buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl [pH 7.5], 1 mM EDTA, and 0.5 M NaCl) and then in low-salt buffer.
L241: Finally, the sample was eluted from the matrix with prewarmed, 65 °C elution buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl [pH 7.5] and 1 mM EDTA). Precipitation of mRNA from eluate (0.5 mL) was performed in potassium-acetate solution (from 50 μL to 5 M [pH 5.0]), glycogen solution (from 10 μL from 20 mg/mL in diethylprocarbonate [DEPC]-treated water), and 95% ethanol (1 mL) for 30 minutes at − 20 °C.
L242: The precipitated mRNA was resuspended in DEPC-treated water, and its concentration was determined spectrophotometrically at 280 nanometers (nm). The isolated mRNA essentially was free of DNA and protein contamination. Aliquots of mRNA in equal concentrations were applied for reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) analysis.
L243: ### RT-PCR
L244: RT-PCR was performed using a OneStep RT-PCR kit (Qiagen Inc.) in accordance with the manufacturer's instruction. The following gene-specific primers were used: abl-FP (24mer), 5′-CTC ATA TCA ACC CGA GTG TCT CTT-3′; abl-RP (24mer), 5′-TGC TAC CTC TGC ACT ATG TCC ATG-3′; bcr-abl fusion-FP (26mer), 5′-GAA GAA GTG TTT CAG AAG CTT CTC CC-3′; and bcr-abl fusion-RP (25mer), 5′-GAC CCG GAG CTT TTC ACC TTT AGT T-3′.
L245: The reverse-transcription reaction was performed at 50 °C for 30 minutes and was followed by HotStar Taq DNA polymerase activation by heating at 95 °C for 15 minutes. Three-step cycling was performed as follows: denaturation for 1 minute at 94 °C, annealing for 1 minute at 50–68 °C, and extension for 1 minute at 72 °C. That 3-step cycle was repeated for 40 cycles followed by a final extension at 72°C for 10 minutes.
L246: cDNA (RT-PCR product) was dissolved in loading buffer and was analyzed by electrophoresis on 1% agarose, precast gel with ethidium bromide (100 V for 30–40 minutes at room temperature [≈ 22 °C]). To ensure that there were no artifacts as a result of the RT-PCR procedure, we also analyzed the expression levels of housekeeper β-actin mRNA in each sample as an endogenous reference using commercially available primers (Qnet).
L247: ### Western Blot Analysis
L248: The cells were treated with ds/siRNAs as described earlier. Aliquots of 4 × 10^{5} cells were lysed in TeloChaser buffer (containing protease and phosphatase inhibitor cocktail; Toyobo Company Ltd., Osaka, Japan) for 30 minutes at 4 °C, centrifuged at × 12,000 g for 20 minutes at 4 °C, and the supernatant fluid was dissolved 1:1 in 2 × Laemmli sample buffer (1.1 M Tris-HCl [pH 6.0], 3.3% sodium dodecyl sulfate [SDS], 22% glycerol, 10% β-mercaptoethanol, and 0.001% bromphenol blue).
L249: Samples (in equal protein concentrations) were heated at 95 °C for 10 minutes and were applied to 5% stacking, 4–12% resolving SDS-polyacrylamide gels. Electrophoresis was performed in 2 steps: at 80 volts (V) for 15 minutes and at 120 V for 2 hours at room temperature. BioRad Kaleidoskop protein standards also were applied for comparison.
L250: After electrophoresis, the separated protein fractions were transferred to a Hybond-P polyvinylidene fluoride membrane (Amersham Bioscience), using XCell II Blot Module (Novex; Wadsworth, OH). The transfer was performed at 35 V for 18 hours at 4 °C. The membranes were cut at the 45-kilodalton (kD) (for β-actin) and 150–210-kD (for c-abl and bcr-abl) molecular weight levels. A double-antibody procedure was used to detect the proteins.
L251: The membranes were incubated under agitation for 1 hour at room temperature in a blocking solution (PBS containing 5% dry skim milk and 0.1% Tween-20), then at room temperature for 1 hour in anti-c-abl (rabbit [Sigma Chemical Company, St. Louis, MO]; 1:100 dilution for bcr-abl 1:500 dilution for c-abl detection) or anti-β-actin monoclonal antibodies (mouse [Calbiochem, Darmstadt, Germany]; 1:20,000 dilution).
L252: The antibody solution was removed, and the membranes were washed 3 times with PBS that contained 0.1% Tween-20. The membranes were then incubated for 1 hour at room temperature under agitation with horseradish peroxidase-conjugated goat antirabbit immunoglobulin G (IgG) (Sigma Chemical Company; 1:5000 dilution) for anti-c-abl and goat antimouse IgM (Sigma Chemical Company; 1:2000 dilution) for anti-β-actin antibody.
L253: Chemiluminescence was detected immediately using the ECL Advanced Western Blotting Detection Kit (Amersham Bioscience).
L254: ### Flow Cytometry
L255: Anti-c-abl antibody (rabbit; Sigma Chemical Company) was labeled using the ZenonAlexa Fluor-488 rabbit IgG Labeling Kit (Molecular Probes Inc., Tokyo, Japan). The permeabilization of cells (treated or nontreated with ds/siRNA) for the Fluor-488-conjugated anti-c-abl antibody was performed using IntraPrep Permeabilization Reagent (Immunotech, Westbrook, ME). The antibody-antigene interaction was detected by flow cytometry (Beckman Coulter-Epics XL; Tokyo, Japan).
L256: Data were collected and analyzed using XL System II software. No cells were excluded from the analysis, and ≈ 5000 cells were counted. The results are presented as a dot plot of Fluor-488 fluorescence (side scatter [y-axis in 0–128 scale] vs. Fluor-488-conjugated antibody [x-axis in 1–1000 scale]) with quadrant markers drawn to distinguish the cells that contained different levels of antibody-antigene complexes.
L257: ### Tyrosine Kinase Activity Test
L258: The cells (treated “chronically” or not treated with ds/siRNA) were sedimented by centrifugation (× 1000 g for 10 minutes), washed twice with PBS (Ca^{2+} and Mg^{2+} free), and resuspended in lysis buffer (TeloChaser; Toyobo Company, Ltd.). The lysis was carried out at 4 °C for 30 minutes in the presence of orthovanadate.
L259: The cytosolic fraction, which contained bcr-abl and/or c-abl, was obtained after centrifugation at × 12,000 g for 10 minutes at 4 °C, and bcr-abl/c-abl proteins were isolated by immunoprecipitation using anti-c-abl antibody (3 μg/mL; Sigma Chemical Company) and protein A/G agarose beads. The protein tyrosine kinase (PTK) activity of immunoprecipitated enzymes was analyzed spectrophotometrically using the Chemicon PTK Assay Kit (with slight modifications).
L260: In brief, a synthetic, biotinylated poly[Glu:Tyr] (4:1; 2.5 μg/mL) containing multiple tyrosine residues was used as a PTK substrate. The PTK reaction was initiated in cell lysates by 1 mM adenosine triphosphate (ATP)/10 mM MgCl_{2} and continued for 60 minutes at 37 °C. After quenching the enzyme reaction with an inhibitor (100 mM EDTA), both the phosphorylated and dephosphorylated substrates were immobilized on streptavidin-coated, 96-well plates.
L261: The fraction of phosphorylated substrate was visualized spectrophotometrically at 450 nm using horseradish peroxidase-conjugated mouse antiphosphotyrosine antibody (clone PY20) and an ensuing chromagenic substrate reaction. The quantity of phosphate incorporated into the tyrosine kinase substrate was determined using the standard phosphopeptide curve.
L262: ### Cell Proliferation Test
L263: Cells (2 × 10^{5} cells/mL) were cultured in the presence or absence of ds/siRNAs, as described earlier. The cell growth was detected spectrophotometrically using the CellTiter AQ Proliferation Assay Kit (Promega, Madison, WI). The method is based on detection of the number of viable cells in proliferation.
L264: A tetrazolium compound (3-[4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl]-5[3-carboxy-methoxyphenyl]-2[4-sulfophenyl]-2H tetrazolium) was bioreduced by cells into a formazan product in the presence of an electron-coupling reagent (phenazine methosulfate), based on the method of Mosmann.cite34†16 The absorbance of formazan product at 490 nm (OD_{490 nm}) was recorded using a 96-well plate reader (InterMedImmunomini NJ-2300; InterMed, Tokyo, Japan).
L265: ### Microarray Analysis
L266: The reverse transcription labeling and hybridization procedures followed the protocol recommended by Agilent Technologies Inc. intended for Agilent microarray analysis. Briefly, a 20 μg aliquot of each mRNA sample was reverse transcribed into a cDNA probe with oligo(dT) primer and labeled nucleotides.
L267: The reaction was performed in a solution that contained 50 μM each of deoxy-ATP, deoxyguanine triphosphate, and deoxythymidine triphosphate; 25 μM deoxycytidine triphosphate (dCTP); 25 μM cyanine 3 (Cy3)-dCTP (for control, nontreated samples) or cyanine 5 (Cy5)-dCTP (for samples that were treated with a ds/siRNA mix for 6 days; Enzo Diagnostics, Inc., Syosset, NY); and 400 U MMLV reverse transcriptase at 42 °C for 1 hour.
L268: The labeling reaction was terminated by incubating the reaction mixture at 70 °C for 10 minutes. The RNA was then degraded by adding 0.05 μg RNaseIA, followed by incubation at 37 °C for 30 minutes. Degraded RNA and unincorporated nucleotides were removed using the QIAquick PCR Purification Kit (Qiagen Inc.) according to the instructions of Agilent Technologies Inc. (Palo Alto, CA).
L269: Hybridization was performed in 22 μL of a hybridization mixture containing cDNA probes, the labeled orientation marker (Deposition Control SP300; Operon Technologies Inc., Alameda, CA), and mouse Cot-1 DNA (Invitrogen) at 65 °C for 17 hours. Next, the glass slides were washed with 0.5 × standard saline citrate (SSC) and 0.01% SDS at room temperature for 5 minutes and then with 0.06 × SSC at room temperature for 2 minutes.
L270: After immediately removing the wash buffer by centrifugation, the glass slides were scanned using GenePix 4000B (Axon Instruments, Inc., Union City, CA) containing a 532-nm laser for Cy3 measurement and a 635-nm laser for Cy5 measurement. Scans were made with a pixel resolution of 5 μm, a laser power of 100%, and a photomultiplier tube voltage of 600 V for the 532-nm laser and 520 V for the 635-nm laser.
L271: ### Normalization and Analysis of Microarray Data
L272: Sixteen-bit TIFF images produced by the Axon scanner were analyzed using the GenePixPro software package (version 3.0; Axon Instruments, Inc.). After obtaining Cy3 and Cy5 gray-scale images, each pseudocolor image was overlaid, and all spots in the ratio image were defined by accessing the gene list file that described the location of each gene on the microarray.
L273: The average of the signal intensity was subtracted from the median of background intensity and outputted with the UniGene and GenBank descriptors to a Microsoft Excel data spreadsheet (Microsoft Corporation, Redmond, WA). Relative expression levels were calculated by global normalization between two samples using all detected genes after the exclusion of spots that were marked as Agilent QC, Agilent blank, and buffer.
L274: ### Statistical Analysis
L275: 
L276: A one-way analysis of variance was employed, followed by a Bonferroni test for truly significant differences. Statistical significance was defined as P values < 0.05. The statistical procedures were performed with GraphPad InStat software (version 2.04; GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA). Data are expressed as means ± standard deviation.
L277: ## RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
L278: The sequences of the originally designed and chemically synthesized ds/siRNAs are shown in Figure cite32†1 A. Three DNA target sequences were chosen, and they were localized in the abl portion of the bcr-abl major breakpoint of Ph chromosome, which is characterized by a bcr exon 3/abl exon 2 (b3a2) junction (a unique sequence in K-562 cells).
L279: The DNA target sequences for the designed ds/siRNA-1 and ds/siRNA-3 were localized in abl exon 3 (they are distinguishing only in 4 bases); and the target sequences for ds/siRNA-2 were localized in abl exon 2. ds/siRNA-4 is a mismatch control (ds/siRNA nonsense).
L280: The selection of DNA target sequences also was intended to avoid the most sensitive area for point mutations in the abl portion of the bcr-abl gene (around Tyr^{315}) that is responsible for bcr-abl amplification and for the development of drug resistance during long-term treatment with conventional antileukemia drugs, as described in clinical trials with imatinib mesylate.cite35†17 , cite36†18 Thus, the designed ds/siRNA constructs have the potential to express their activity if they are applied in combination with imatinib mesylate during long-term treatment of bcr-abl-positive cells.
